name: ATP6AP1-CDG (Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation, ATP6AP1 type)

clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive type II congenital disorder of glycosylation affecting predominantly males, caused by loss-of-function variants in ATP6AP1, an accessory subunit of the vacuolar-type H+-ATPase (V-ATPase).
The combination of immunodeficiency, hepatopathy and cutis laxa, often with cognitive impairment, is characteristic and should prompt consideration of a Golgi-homeostasis CDG.
Humoral immunodeficiency with hypogammaglobulinaemia and recurrent bacterial infections means some boys present first to immunology rather than to metabolic services.
Liver involvement spans raised transaminases and cholestasis through to progressive fibrosis and cirrhosis, with a tendency to decompensate during intercurrent illness.
Serum copper and caeruloplasmin may be low, reflecting disturbed Golgi metal handling, and can mimic a primary copper-metabolism disorder.
Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing typically shows a type II (glycan-processing) pattern, distinguishing it from the commoner type I disorders.
Connective-tissue laxity and cutis laxa link it to the wider V-ATPase and Golgi-homeostasis group of glycosylation defects.
reference.pathophysiology: The ATP6AP1 gene on Xq28 encodes an accessory subunit (Ac45) of the multi-subunit vacuolar H+-ATPase, the proton pump that acidifies the lumen of the Golgi apparatus, endosomes and lysosomes. Loss-of-function variants impair assembly and activity of the V-ATPase, so Golgi luminal pH is no longer correctly maintained; because the terminal, pH-sensitive glycosyltransferases and the trafficking of metal ions such as manganese and copper depend on proper Golgi acidification, protein N- and O-glycosylation is disturbed in a type II processing pattern. The resulting hypoglycosylation of secreted and membrane glycoproteins, including immunoglobulins and hepatic proteins, underlies the humoral immunodeficiency, the hepatopathy, the abnormal copper and caeruloplasmin handling and the connective-tissue (cutis laxa) features.
additionalDifferentials: ATP6AP2-CDG (related V-ATPase accessory-protein defect with hepatopathy and immune features)
ATP6V0A2-CDG (autosomal recessive cutis laxa type IIA)
ATP6V1A-CDG and ATP6V1E1-CDG (V-ATPase core-subunit cutis laxa disorders)
CCDC115-CDG and TMEM199-CDG (Golgi-homeostasis CDGs with hepatopathy and low caeruloplasmin)
Wilson disease and Menkes disease (copper-metabolism mimics)
Common variable immunodeficiency and other primary humoral immunodeficiencies
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing / glycoform analysis (expect a type II pattern)
Quantitative immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subset analysis
Liver function tests, coagulation profile and hepatic ultrasound or elastography
Molecular testing of ATP6AP1 with an X-linked/CDG gene panel or exome sequencing
Mass spectrometry glycomics of N- and O-linked glycans
Liver biopsy where hepatic disease is progressive or unexplained
redFlags: Rapid hepatic decompensation or coagulopathy during intercurrent infection
Severe or recurrent bacterial sepsis attributable to hypogammaglobulinaemia
Signs of portal hypertension or advancing cirrhosis
Bleeding tendency from combined hepatic and glycosylation-related coagulation-factor deficiency
reference.prognosis: Outlook is variable and is driven largely by the severity of the liver disease and of infections; some individuals stabilise with immunoglobulin replacement and supportive hepatic care, whereas progressive cirrhosis or overwhelming infection can be life-threatening.
pitfalls: Labelling the picture as isolated hypogammaglobulinaemia in an immunology clinic and missing the underlying glycosylation defect.
Misinterpreting low copper and caeruloplasmin as Wilson or Menkes disease.
Being falsely reassured by a normal first-line type I transferrin screen, since a type II pattern requires specific glycoform analysis.
Overlooking carrier mothers and milder female phenotypes because the disorder is X-linked.
references: Physician's Guide to the Diagnosis, Treatment and Follow-up of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
Congenital disorders of glycosylation: clinical and diagnostic reviews
